title: CoreWeave: the backlog is real; the equity is a levered bet on refinancing it
subtitle: Initiation. Revenue is compounding at more than 110% a year against a US$104bn backlog, but most of the build-out is funded with borrowed money that the bond market now prices near distress. Our four scenarios run from a restructuring (about US$0) to about US$259 a share. Weighted, they give about US$70, 14% above the US$61.39 close, with a 55% chance of losing three-quarters of the equity or more. We start at Neutral, with Very high risk.
author: GIVA Research (AI-assisted)

stance.label: Neutral
stance.horizon: About 14 months, to end-2027 (our valuation date). Checkpoints: Q3 FY2026 results (around 9–10 Nov 2026) and FY2026 results with the FY2027 capex guide (around late Feb 2027)
stance.summary: The fundamentals are not the problem: Q2 FY2026 revenue rose **112% y/y** to US$2.58bn and RPO reached **US$103.7bn** [s2,s8]. The funding is: net debt of about **US$29.8bn** on **US$5.0bn** of equity [s8,s57], interest of US$640m a quarter heading to about US$900m [s9], and unsecured bonds yielding about 15% [s28,s31]. Our probability-weighted value is about **US$70** a share against the US$61.39 close [s25], but 55% of the weight sits in a restructuring or a funding-constrained bear case that leaves the equity worth US$5 or less. Whether CoreWeave can fund its 2027 plan on acceptable terms will largely be settled inside our horizon, and we have no edge over the credit market on that, so we start at Neutral.

highlights: **Fundamental growth is not the debate.** Revenue rose from US$229m in FY2023 to US$5.13bn in FY2025 and US$7.59bn TTM; Q2 FY2026 grew 112% y/y, and FY2026 guidance was raised to US$12.4–13.2bn [s1,s2,s9].

**Financing is the debate.** TTM operating cash flow of US$6.9bn covered about a third of US$20.6bn of cash capex, and the company plans US$35–39bn of capex in 2026 on its own definition [s2,s9]. Interest expense rose from US$267m (Q2 FY2025) to US$640m (Q2 FY2026), with US$860–940m guided for Q3 [s8,s9].

**The October slide started in the credit market, but it is not only sentiment.** Shares fell about 25% in the week to 16 Oct as unsecured yields reached about 15% and five-year CDS hit a record of about 1,195bp intraday [s27,s28,s34]. For a company that can only grow by borrowing, the cost of funding is a fundamental input, and two demand datapoints turned too: OpenAI’s lower net revenue run-rate and Reuters’ report of hyperscaler capex-delay signals [s35,s47]. Reported results did not miss.

**Valuation is a levered residual with a real tail.** Our base case (FY2028 adj. EBITDA US$23.6bn at 7x, net debt about US$77bn by end-2027) is worth about US$120 a share; a funding-constrained bear case about US$5; a restructuring about nothing. Weighted 15/40/35/10 with the bull case (about US$259), that is about US$70. Each turn of EV/EBITDA moves the base case by about US$32 a share.

**Revenue concentration is falling; backlog concentration is not.** The largest customer fell from 71% to 36% of revenue in a year, but on disclosed contract ceilings Meta (about US$35bn) and OpenAI (about US$22bn) are roughly a third and a fifth of the US$103.7bn RPO. OpenAI-backed capacity is financed in a non-investment-grade facility that cannot use the A3-rated DDTL 4.0 template [s2,s17,s19,s103,s110].

blocks.text: CoreWeave rents NVIDIA GPU capacity, mostly on multi-year take-or-pay contracts, to AI labs and hyperscalers [s1,s84]. Revenue was **US$5.13bn in FY2025 (+168%)** and **US$2.58bn in Q2 FY2026 alone (+112% y/y)** [s1,s2]. Contracted demand is visible: RPO was **US$103.7bn** at 30 June 2026, and management reported more than US$25bn of further commitments signed early in Q3 [s2,s8].

The equity case turns on the other side of the balance sheet. Most of the build-out is financed with debt raised against GPUs and customer contracts: operating cash flow covered about a third of cash capex over the last twelve months, and NVIDIA added US$2bn of equity in January [s2,s62]. Debt was about **US$35.1bn** at 30 June 2026 against **US$5.0bn** of equity [s2,s57]. Interest already exceeds adjusted operating income: US$640m against US$128m in Q2 [s8], with Q3 guidance of US$860–940m against US$200–260m [s9]. S&P rates the issuer B+, with a positive outlook [s117]. The company is exposed less to demand than to the price and availability of credit, and in October that price moved sharply against it [s28,s31].

items.label: Risk
items.value: Very high: book equity is about 6.5% of assets, and 55% of our scenario weight loses three-quarters of the equity or more

items.label: Probability-weighted value (15/40/35/10)
items.value: ≈ US$70 a share against a US$61.39 close [s25] (Section 8)

items.label: Credit-market read, like for like
items.value: five-year CDS near 1,040bp implies about a 16% one-year and 58% five-year risk-neutral default probability at 40% recovery (our arithmetic from [s31]); we put 15% on a restructuring by end-2027

blocks.text: **Why Neutral.** Our weighted value is about 14% above the share price, but the distribution is close to binary: 55% of the weight sits in a restructuring or in a funding-constrained bear case worth about US$5, and 45% in cases worth about US$120–260. Which side CoreWeave lands on turns on funding roughly US$50bn of cash needs through end-2027 (Section 8), and the answer will largely be known inside our horizon, once the FY2027 capex and funding plan is out. We have no edge over the credit market on that outcome, and small changes in our weights move the weighted value by about as much as the gap to the price: each 5 points moved from the bear to the base case adds about US$6. To stress-test these assumptions, including the interest-rate path, use the interactive model in Section 9. **Why not Cautious.** Reported results have not missed: Q2 beat consensus revenue, guidance went up and the backlog grew [s8,s24]. A successful investment-grade financing of the 2027 plan would cut the cost of capital sharply (DDTL 4.0 priced at SOFR + 225bp [s17]).

blocks.title: What would make us more positive
blocks.text: Q3 FY2026 revenue at or above the US$3.45–3.60bn guide with interest inside US$860–940m [s9]; an FY2027 capex plan funded mainly through investment-grade, contract-backed facilities like DDTL 4.0 rather than unsecured paper near 15% [s17,s28]; an upgrade from S&P’s B+ toward the investment-grade profile management says it is targeting [s109,s117]; and a sustained fall in CDS from the October record [s31].

blocks.title: What would make us Cautious
blocks.text: Refinancing at unsecured yields near current levels; any cash-trap event under a GPU facility [s61]; another capex raise without matching revenue; re-scoping of an OpenAI or Microsoft contract [s35]; another data-centre delivery delay like November 2025’s [s114]; or equity issuance well beyond the 35m-share at-the-market programme [s109].

**Model.** CoreWeave sells GPU compute by the hour or, mostly, under committed multi-year contracts. Average contract length rose from about four to about five years during 2025 [s84]. Customers prepay part of the contract value, which is why deferred revenue reached US$9.7bn at 30 June 2026 [s2]. Each large contract is typically financed in its own special-purpose vehicle with a delayed-draw term loan (DDTL) secured on the GPUs and the contract cash flows, which pay operating costs and lenders before the parent [s17,s103]. One secondary source describes a cash trap in DDTL 3.0 if a key customer seriously breaches its contract [s61]; we have not checked that against the credit agreement. In Q3 FY2026 the company began signing short-dated (3–6 month) capacity at about US$40m of annualised revenue per MW, which it described as higher pricing [s16,s37]. For scale, Q2 revenue ran at about US$7m a year per active MW (US$2.58bn × 4 ÷ about 1.5 GW, our arithmetic [s2,s10]); most existing capacity is locked in at fixed contract prices, so the uplift reaches revenue slowly.

**Platform.** Beyond bare-metal GPUs, the stack includes CoreWeave Kubernetes Service, Slurm-on-Kubernetes (SUNK), Mission Control for fleet operations, and developer tools from acquisitions: Weights & Biases (completed May 2025) [s22], OpenPipe and Marimo [s102]. A planned all-stock takeover of Core Scientific was voted down by that company’s shareholders on 30 October 2025 [s23]. CoreWeave still leases about 590 MW from Core Scientific across six sites under 12-year hosting contracts [s115], which makes it the company’s largest landlord.

blocks.caption: Footprint and power
blocks.note: Active power was about 41% of contracted power at 30 June 2026 (our arithmetic): most of the contracted capacity still has to be built, energised and financed. Capacity is mostly leased colocation; the first self-built site is due in 2026 [s81].

blocks.text: **NVIDIA is supplier, shareholder, customer and backstop at once.** It supplies the GPUs, anchored the IPO and invested a further US$2bn at US$87.20 a share in January 2026 [s62,s63]. Under a September 2025 order it must buy any capacity CoreWeave cannot sell, up to US$6.3bn through April 2032 [s20]. On 15 October its CEO said CoreWeave was "improving every day" and needed no backstop [s32]. The arrangement supports demand in a downturn, but it also ties CoreWeave’s fortunes to a single supplier’s strategy.

**Governance.** Class B shares carry ten votes. At 31 July 2026 Class B was about 17% of shares and about 67% of votes, held by the founders [s55]. Founders and early investors have been heavy sellers since the IPO, mostly under 10b5-1 plans [s53,s96].

**Controls and litigation.** The FY2025 10-K reports material weaknesses in internal control over financial reporting (IT general controls, segregation of duties and accounting staffing) that still existed at 31 December 2025, with remediation expected to continue through 2026 [s1]. Every statement figure in this report rests on those filings. A securities class action (Masaitis v. CoreWeave, D.N.J. No. 2:26-cv-00355, class period 28 March to 15 December 2025) alleges the company understated its reliance on a single third-party data-centre supplier; we have not tracked its current status [s116].

**Demand.** The four largest US platforms (Amazon, Microsoft, Alphabet, Meta) guided combined 2026 capex of roughly US$700–725bn, up from about US$410bn in 2025 [s78]. Neoclouds take the overflow, and Microsoft has been CoreWeave’s largest customer [s56]. Frontier labs (OpenAI, Meta, Anthropic) are the other demand pool [s18,s19,s92].

**Doubts.** In October the sector’s sentiment turned on three things. OpenAI told investors its annualised revenue was about US$50bn, below the widely reported US$68bn, which had counted revenue booked by its partners [s35]. Reuters reported hints of data-centre project delays and slower capex growth from hyperscalers, and that Gartner ranks CoreWeave first of about 100 neoclouds on exposure to the gap between revenue and capital spending [s47]. And Gartner forecast that more than 80% of neocloud providers will be forced to cease independent operations by 2030 [s29,s30].

blocks.text: **Where CoreWeave is strong.** It has the largest backlog, it is usually first to deploy new NVIDIA platforms, and it was first to raise investment-grade financing against GPU contracts (DDTL 4.0, rated A3 by Moody’s and backed by Meta contracts) [s17,s60]. **Where it is weak.** It owns little of its real estate or power, its cost of unsecured capital is high, and two counterparties hold most of its disclosed backlog (Section 6).

**Power and delivery.** Delivery risk is not theoretical. On 10 November 2025 CoreWeave cut FY2025 revenue guidance from US$5.15–5.35bn to US$5.05–5.15bn because a third-party data-centre developer (reported to be Core Scientific) ran late, and the shares fell sharply the next day [s13,s114]; FY2025 revenue landed at US$5.13bn [s1]. With active power at about 41% of contracted power at 30 June 2026 (Section 2), most of the backlog still depends on landlords and utilities delivering on time. Our bear case assumes they deliver late and the company cannot fund the rest at acceptable cost.

**GPU useful life: how much of the EBITDA is real?** CoreWeave depreciates technology equipment over six years [s1]; secondary coverage reports that it lengthened that life from five to six years from 1 January 2023, which we have not confirmed in the filings [s85]. Critics argue the economic life of AI GPUs is closer to two or three years [s85]. Depreciation is the largest cost line: about US$1.4bn in Q2 FY2026, 54% of revenue [s2]. The table rescales Q2 depreciation to shorter lives, holding everything else equal.

blocks.caption: Q2 FY2026 depreciation and operating income at shorter GPU lives (US$ m, our arithmetic)
blocks.note: A simple rescaling: it treats all depreciation as technology equipment on a six-year straight-line life (buildings and other assets have different lives), and Q2 depreciation is itself filed rounded (about ±US$100m). Cash flow does not change.

blocks.text: A shorter life does not change cash flow, but it changes two things that matter here. First, maintenance: to hold a given EBITDA, the fleet has to be replaced on its economic life, not its book life, so EBITDA overstates owner earnings by the gap. Second, collateral: GPU loans are sized against contracts of about five years and amortise from contract cash flows [s17,s84], so lenders are exposed to what a GPU is worth when its first contract ends. If renewal prices for Hopper-generation fleets reset sharply lower, the residual value that the next financing leans on falls with them. We reflect this in a below-peer 7x base multiple and in the bear case’s lower FY2028 margin (Section 8) rather than in a DCF.

All statement figures below come from CoreWeave’s XBRL filings with the SEC, processed by GIVA’s deterministic financials job. Revenue, operating income and net income match the company’s press releases to rounding for every quarter we checked [s8,s11,s12,s13]. The company reported material weaknesses in internal control over financial reporting at 31 December 2025 (Section 2) [s1], so we use the filings as filed and mark figures that rest on rounded inputs. Two definitional differences matter, and we show both versions: **capex** (XBRL records cash paid; the company’s headline figure also includes accrued and vendor-financed additions) and **EBITDA** (our GAAP proxy versus the company’s adjusted figure).

blocks.title: Quarterly operating income and net income (GAAP)

blocks.text: **Fundamental growth troughed at about 110%, and guidance implies re-acceleration.** Year-on-year revenue growth fell from 420% in Q1 FY2025 to 110% in Q4 FY2025, then held at 112% in each of the first two quarters of 2026. Sequential growth picked up to 32% in Q1 FY2026 and 24% in Q2 [s2,s3]. The Q3 guide midpoint of US$3.53bn implies about 158% y/y and 37% q/q, and the FY2026 midpoint of US$12.8bn about 149% [s9]. The debate is whether the second-half ramp is delivered on time, given the November 2025 delay (Section 3).

blocks.note: Percentage growth is shown only off a positive base; where the base is a loss, the absolute change is shown instead. Where an input is rounded (depreciation from Q3 FY2025), EBITDA-proxy growth is shown as the range the rounding allows. Growth here is always fundamental (revenue, gross profit, EBITDA), never share-price performance.

blocks.text: **Margins are compressing.** Revenue less cost of revenue (which excludes depreciation) fell from about 73–76% through Q3 FY2025 to 67.6% in Q4 FY2025 and about 66% in the first half of 2026. We have not confirmed management’s explanation; the likeliest driver is lease and power cost on capacity that is energised before it earns full revenue (operating lease cost was about US$500m in Q2 FY2026, against about US$180m a year earlier, per the 10-Q [s2]). Gross-profit growth (88% y/y in Q2 FY2026) is now well below revenue growth (112%). Operating margin was negative in three of the last four quarters, because depreciation arrives as soon as capacity is energised, before the revenue ramps [s2].

blocks.text: **Cash flow and capex intensity.** Over the twelve months to June 2026, operating cash flow was US$6.9bn (91% of revenue, flattered by customer prepayments) and cash capex was US$20.6bn (271% of revenue), for free cash flow of **−US$13.7bn** [s2]. On the company’s capex definition the burn is larger: H1 FY2026 company-defined capex was about US$17.1bn against US$3.7bn of operating cash flow [s2,s8,s83]. The full-year plan of US$35–39bn means roughly US$20bn more to fund in the second half [s9].

blocks.title: Operating cash flow vs cash capex by quarter
The capex treadmill
blocks.text: Capex guidance for 2026 was raised twice, from US$30–35bn to US$31–35bn in May and to US$35–39bn in August, while revenue guidance rose only at the edges [s9,s83]. At midpoints, the August revision added about US$13 of capex for each US$1 of added revenue guidance [s9,s98]. Part of that capex is for revenue in 2027 and beyond, but until the ratio turns, every revenue beat brings a larger financing need.

blocks.text: **Interest burden.** Interest expense rose from US$361m in FY2024 to US$1,229m in FY2025 and US$640m in Q2 FY2026 alone, against US$267m a year earlier [s8,s12]. Q3 guidance of US$860–940m is about four times guided adjusted operating income of US$200–260m [s9]. Measured against adjusted EBITDA, interest absorbed 40% in FY2025 and 42% in Q2 FY2026 (our arithmetic from [s8,s12]). Fixed-charge cover is thin: in Q2, adjusted EBITDA plus rent covered interest plus rent about 1.8 times (our arithmetic from [s2,s8]). Because most secured debt floats over SOFR, rates feed straight into the interest line: the Fed raised its target range by 25bp to 3.75–4.00% on 16 September, its first hike since 2023 [s111], and the hot September CPI print raised the odds of another move at the 27–28 October meeting [s87].

**Maturities and liquidity.** US$7.5bn of debt was classified as current at 30 June 2026 [s57], and one secondary source puts principal due by end-2027 at US$10.6bn [s58]. DDTL debt amortises from contract cash flows, so the more relevant refinancing exposure is the unsecured notes and any facility whose cash is trapped. The company did breach covenants on a 2024 loan, which triggered technical defaults that were later waived [s91]. Cash was US$5.5bn at 30 June. The September convertible closed at US$4.2bn with the option exercised: net proceeds were about US$4.14bn, and after about US$0.57bn of capped calls it added about US$3.57bn of cash before offering expenses [s39,s108].

**Dilution.** Class A plus Class B shares were 551.5m at 31 July 2026, up from 545.6m at 30 April [s3,s55]; implied weighted basic shares were 200.7m in FY2024 and 424.4m in FY2025 (IPO and conversions) [s1]. Ahead: the ATM programme (up to 35m shares, about 6% of the count) [s109]; three convertibles, of which the 2033s convert into about 42.9m shares at US$97.85 and the 2032s into roughly 33m at about US$119.60 (the 2031s’ conversion terms we have not confirmed), each with capped calls that offset dilution up to their caps [s14,s105,s106,s107]; and stock-based compensation of US$619m over the last twelve months, 8.2% of revenue [s2]. We treat all three convertibles as debt in every scenario (Section 8).

blocks.title: Credit market, week of 12–16 October
blocks.text: The 9.625% 2032 notes traded below 80 cents for a yield near 15%, and the 2031s yielded about 15.8% on 15 October [s28,s31]. Five-year CDS reached a record of about 1,195bp intraday before settling near 1,040bp [s31,s34]. S&P rates the issuer B+ with a positive outlook [s117]. Equity holders sit below roughly US$35bn of debt at 30 June, more after the September convertible, that the market prices as high yield bordering on distressed. Section 8 sets the equity discount rate separately from these yields.

blocks.title: Remaining performance obligations (RPO) and deferred revenue

blocks.text: RPO rose from US$14.7bn at March 2025 to **US$103.7bn** at June 2026, about **13.7x TTM revenue** [s2,s6]. The company’s "revenue backlog" (RPO plus other committed amounts) was about US$104bn, excluding more than US$25bn of commitments signed after quarter-end [s8]. At Q1 the company said about 36% of backlog would be recognised within 24 months [s95]. On the Q2 call management said ten customers have each committed at least US$1bn, and that non-investment-grade AI-native companies and labs are under 30% of backlog [s10,s86].

blocks.text: **Our read.** Revenue concentration is falling; backlog concentration is not. The largest customer fell from 71% of revenue a year ago to 36% in Q2 FY2026 [s2,s56], but in dollars it barely moved (about US$0.86bn in Q2 FY2025 against about US$0.93bn in Q2 FY2026, if Customer A is the same company in both periods), so the falling share reflects growth elsewhere rather than roll-off. We have not reviewed Microsoft’s contract end dates in the 10-K. On the backlog, two counterparties hold more than half of the disclosed ceilings. The bear reading: about US$22bn of ceilings from OpenAI, whose own disclosure put its net annualised revenue at about US$50bn rather than the US$68bn gross figure that had been reported [s35], sit in non-investment-grade financing that cannot migrate to the SOFR + 225bp structure, which works only because Meta is investment grade [s17,s103]. Large RPO is necessary for the equity case, but on its own it does not make the case.

sections.title: Recent share-price performance: what drove the slide

blocks.text: From a post-earnings close of about US$108 on 12 August (a single source) [s40] the shares fell to **US$61.39 on 16 October** [s25,s26], about **−43%**. Most of the fall came in the week of 12–16 October, when the shares lost about a quarter of their value [s27]. CNBC’s quote page showed a 52-week high of US$150.40, set on 16 October 2025, so that high was rolling out of the window on our data date [s42]. The October slide also retraced a rebound: the shares had fallen about 26% in the five sessions to 29 July [s113] before rallying on the August results. Since August the move had three legs: a five-session fall of about 19% to 15 September, ahead of the Fed’s 16 September hike [s111,s112]; the convertible-plus-ATM financing on 17 September; and an October cascade that started in the credit market.

blocks.text: **Interpretation.** The slide started in the credit market: unsecured yields moved from 9–10% coupons to about 15% and CDS reached a record [s28,s31]. That is not only sentiment. For a company that can only grow by borrowing, the cost and availability of funding are fundamental inputs, and two demand datapoints also turned against it: OpenAI’s lower net run-rate and Reuters’ hyperscaler capex-delay signals [s35,s47]. Reported results did not miss: the last quarter beat on revenue and raised guidance [s8,s24]. The fall was also sector-wide: Nebius, IREN, Oracle and the semiconductor index fell alongside, and CoreWeave, the most levered name, fell most [s25,s48]. Sell-side defenders included Cantor (Overweight, US$176), JPMorgan ("overdone") and Deutsche Bank [s46,s70,s93].

CoreWeave has no earnings to put a P/E on, so we value it on enterprise value against forward adjusted EBITDA, and we treat the equity explicitly as what is left after debt. Spot inputs: **US$61.39** close [s25] × **551.5m** shares [s55] = **US$33.9bn** market cap; plus **US$29.8bn** net debt at 30 June [s57] = **US$63.6bn** spot EV (our arithmetic). We treat all three convertibles as debt, assuming net-share settlement: principal is repaid like debt, and the capped calls offset the conversion spread up to their caps [s14,s106].

blocks.note: CoreWeave’s adjusted EBITDA adds back all stock-based compensation and sits above depreciation equal to about 40–55% of revenue, so its EBITDA multiples are not like-for-like with asset-light peers [s77]. We found no citable EV/EBITDA for the hyperscalers and do not show one.

blocks.text: **Choosing the multiple.** The asset-light names above are not the right anchor: their EBITDA is not consumed by depreciation and their balance sheets are investment grade. The closer economic comparables are lessors of depreciating, debt-financed equipment on contracts (aircraft lessors, equipment rental), with contracted data-centre landlords as an upper bound for longer-dated contracts on longer-lived assets. We did not find dated, citable multiples for those groups in time for this report, so we show none. Our 7x base multiple is about Oracle’s next-twelve-months multiple (8.6x FY May-2027 and 6.0x FY May-2028 on 18 October, ~7.2x blended [s72]) and well below the asset-light peers; the bear case uses 5.5x, a distressed-credit level.

**Method.** We value the company at end-2027 on a one-year-forward multiple of FY2028 adjusted EBITDA, roll net debt forward with guidance and consensus cash flows, and discount the per-share value back 1.2 years at an **18% cost of equity**. That rate is a stated premium (roughly the 3.75–4.00% policy rate [s111] plus about 14 points for a single-B, pre-profit, highly levered equity), not a read-across from the bond yield: a 15% yield on near-distressed bonds is a promised yield, not an expected return. Default risk sits in the scenario weights, so the high rate is partly a second, conservative haircut; at 15% or 21% the weighted value would be about US$72 or US$68. Step 1 is common to all cases: from US$29.8bn at 30 June, H2 FY2026 company-defined capex of about US$19.9bn (guide midpoint US$37bn less H1 about US$17.1bn [s9,s83,s8]), H2 adjusted EBITDA of about US$4.7bn (consensus FY US$7.4bn [s65] less H1 US$2.67bn [s8,s11]), interest of about US$1.9bn and US$1.5bn of prepayments take **net debt to about US$45.3bn by end-2026**. After that, any equity raised is credited against net debt, so new shares are not counted twice. Section 9 puts these inputs on sliders; its base case gives about US$114 a share, lower mainly because it pays stock-based compensation in new shares.

rows.name: Restructuring
rows.text: Unsecured refinancing fails, or a covenant or cash-trap event cascades, before the FY2027 plan is funded, and the equity is wiped out or heavily diluted in a restructuring. We set the weight a little below the roughly 19% risk-neutral default probability that CDS near 1,040bp implies to end-2027 at 40% recovery [s31], because risk-neutral odds overstate real-world ones. D.A. Davidson has said the equity "could go to zero" [s43].

rows.name: Bear
rows.text: Funding-constrained. Capital stays expensive, so FY2027 capex is cut to about US$22bn; revenue stalls near the exit-2026 run-rate (US$20bn in FY2027, US$22bn in FY2028); renewal pricing on Hopper fleets resets lower and leased capacity sits part-empty (52% FY2028 margin). Net debt still reaches about US$59bn, 5.1x FY2028 EBITDA, and at a distressed 5.5x the equity is a sliver spread over 90m more shares. Triggers: refinancing near 15%, a large customer re-scoping, or another delivery delay [s28,s35,s114].

rows.name: Base
rows.text: Consensus-like FY27 revenue of US$26.3bn, 62% margins, and FY28 adjusted EBITDA of about US$23.6bn valued at 7x, about Oracle’s next-twelve-months multiple [s64,s72]. Requires the 2027 capex plan (about US$47bn) to be funded without a further jump in the cost of capital; the 35m-share ATM is sold at about US$70.

rows.name: Bull
rows.text: Revenue at the top of the range (US$31bn in FY27, US$45bn in FY28), 65% margins as short-term pricing holds [s16], and a re-rating to 9x as investment-grade financing becomes the norm [s17]. Net debt still rises to about US$76bn, about 2.6x FY2028 EBITDA.

"<0" means enterprise value below net debt: the equity cannot be worth less than nothing, and that corner is the restructuring case. That gearing is why the equity moves several times as much as the bonds.

blocks.text: **Does the backlog cover the debt on its own?** We test the "backlog is real" half of the thesis by stopping growth: no capex after the committed 2026 build, revenue held at the roughly US$19bn exit-2026 run-rate [s9] for five years (about the average contract length [s84]), a 59% EBITDA margin [s8], and the US$9.7bn of customer prepayments already received [s2] unwinding over the period. Contracted cash flow pays the interest and cuts net debt from about US$45bn to about US$18bn by end-2031, but it does not clear it. In run-off, the equity is worth roughly the residual value of five-year-old GPUs plus the value of renewing contracts, less about US$18bn of debt, before discounting. The backlog is real; on its own it does not make the equity safe.

blocks.text: This section turns the report’s assumptions into a working model. Pick a scenario, move a slider or choose a SOFR path, and the FY2026E–FY2030E P&L, funding need, debt, interest, covenant tests, forward multiples and value per share recalculate in the browser; **Copy link** keeps the exact settings. FY2026E is the reported first half [s2] plus the model’s second half, held at guidance in every preset [s9]. The opening balance sheet is the 30 June 10-Q; August’s DDTL 5.5 and revolver draws and September’s US$4.2bn convertible enter on their dates [s2,s14]. The base case uses FY2026 guidance, consensus-like FY2027 revenue [s64] and Section 8’s FY2028, passes the FY2026 guidance and FY2027 consensus checks (Calibration tab) and gives **about US$114 a share**, against Section 8’s ≈US$120: the model pays stock-based compensation in new shares at today’s price (630m shares at end-2027, against 600m) and draws about US$9.9bn of committed facilities before new borrowing at about 10.5%. The Restructuring, Bear, Base and Bull presets give about US$0, US$5, US$114 and US$245; weighted 15/40/35/10 that is **about US$66**, close to Section 8’s ≈US$70. The bull is below Section 8’s US$259 because it counts about 29m net convertible shares above the capped-call caps. Four more presets stress rates and credit.

**Interest rates and the P&L.** Each +100bp on SOFR (from November 2026) adds about US$0.41bn to FY2027E and US$0.81bn to FY2028E interest, because by end-2028 about 78% of the debt floats or is new borrowing that reprices. The same move takes about US$10 off value per share, mostly by re-rating the exit multiple as the cost of capital rises (7.0x to 6.7x). The SOFR path selector runs market forwards [s122], the Fed’s September projections [s119,s120,s121] or two stress paths of our own. On the Fed path FY2028E interest is US$8.6bn against US$9.1bn and value about US$120; on the re-hike path it is US$9.5bn and about US$107. SOFR +150bp with spreads +100bp lifts FY2027E interest from US$5.6bn to US$6.5bn and FY2028E to US$11.0bn, and cuts value to about US$90; new financing at 14% instead of 10.5% gives about US$82. **What moves FY2027E net income** (base about −US$3.4bn, or −US$5.65 a share against consensus of −US$4.49 [s64]): GPU depreciation life (4 to 7 years: −US$9.3bn to −US$1.7bn, with no change in cash), how fast new capex enters service (0.1 to 0.75 years: −US$5.7bn to −US$0.9bn), revenue growth (−20 to +10 points: −US$4.9bn to −US$2.6bn) and the cost of new debt (9% to 14%: −US$3.1bn to −US$4.2bn). FY2028E net income (about −US$8.1bn) sits well below published estimates of −US$1.2bn to −US$2.6bn [s65,s140], mostly because Section 8’s FY2028 EBITDA of US$23.6bn is below the US$28.7bn consensus [s65]; the Calibration tab shows that miss rather than hiding it. **Value per share** swings most with the exit multiple (5x to 9x: US$52 to US$174), revenue growth (US$63 to US$141), the cost of equity (US$159 to US$82) and the cost of new debt (US$130 to US$82). **What the price implies** (Breakevens tab): at US$61.39 the shares are worth what the model says only at 5.3x FY2028 EBITDA (we assume 7x), at revenue growth about 21 points a year below the path, or with new financing at about 17%.

blocks.title: How interest expense is projected
blocks.text: **Rate paths.** SOFR follows market forwards as of 15 October 2026: 3.85% for H2 2026, then 4.45%, 4.65%, 4.60% and 4.45% (2030 is our assumption) [s122,s111]. The Fed’s September projections run 0, 35, 65, 85 and 100bp below that in 2026–30 [s119,s120,s121]; the path selector and the “Fed projections path” preset apply them year by year, and July–October 2026 is treated as realised. **Fixed vs floating.** Of US$42.2bn of principal (US$35.6bn at 30 June [s2], plus August’s US$1.2bn DDTL 5.5 and US$1.2bn revolver draws [s2] and September’s US$4.2bn 2.875% convertible [s14]), about US$13.5bn (32%) floats over SOFR: DDTL 1.0, 2.0, 2.1, 3.0 and 5.5, the DDTL 4.0 floating tranche and the revolver [s127,s128,s129,s103,s17,s59]. DDTL 5.0 must be at least 95% swapped and is treated as fixed [s104]. DDTL 4.0 must hedge at least 95% of its floating draws after mid-2027; the model does not, so it slightly overstates the floating sensitivity from then on. The rest is fixed: senior notes at 8.5–9.75% [s130,s131,s132,s133,s134], convertibles at 1.75–2.875% and OEM financing at about 9–11% [s2]. Each tranche pays its stated rate on its balance month by month. Issue-cost and discount amortisation (about US$0.1–0.25bn a year) is carried as non-cash interest, as the income statement does, and added back in cash flow. Amortising loans follow a schedule fitted to the 10-Q maturity table [s2]. **Funding.** Any gap (capex and repayments not covered by operating cash flow, keeping US$4bn of cash) is first drawn from about US$9.9bn of committed, undrawn facilities on their own terms (DDTL 4.0, 5.0 and 5.5 and the revolver [s2,s17,s104,s59]). The rest is borrowed at the new-debt rate: about 10.5% at base, a mix of secured DDTL-style debt at the latest SOFR + 5.50% pricing [s59], OEM financing, unsecured notes near their October yields [s28,s31] and converts. It moves with the selected path and the SOFR and spread sliders; credit spreads never touch contractual margins. Uncommitted funding reaches about US$43bn by end-2027 and US$81bn by end-2028, so most of the rate risk sits in debt not yet raised. **Covenants.** The unsecured notes reportedly cap total leverage at 6.0x and secured leverage at 4.0x [s137]. Base total debt is 6.8x FY2026E EBITDA, above the cap, then 5.2x in FY2027 and 4.8x in FY2028; the bear case is back above it, at 7.0x, in FY2028.

blocks.title: What the model leaves out
blocks.text: Presets keep FY2026 at guidance and shift FY2027–30 by the same amount each year. Revenue follows in-service capacity, so cutting capex costs revenue a few quarters later; the bear preset sets revenue directly and switches that link off. There are no tax-loss carry-forwards (a tax charge of about US$290m a year stands in for the tax CoreWeave books in loss years), no interest on cash, no capitalised interest and no default mechanics: below zero, the equity value simply floors at nothing, and a covenant breach is flagged rather than stopping the borrowing. Convertibles are debt at face, with net shares only above their capped-call caps. It is a tool for testing assumptions, not a forecast.

sections.title: Appendix: what our systematic screens said

blocks.title: Short answer: nothing flagged it
blocks.text: No GIVA module named CoreWeave, flagged its share-price slide, or warned about the balance-sheet and credit risk behind it before the week of 12–16 October. CoreWeave has never appeared on the published dashboard [s99]. The miss is structural: several independent gaps each blocked it, and fixing any single one would not have produced the call.

The only related signal was generic and at market level. In every weekly run between 1 August and 12 October (nine runs; none was recorded for 17, 24 or 31 August), our market models flagged the Nasdaq, S&P 500, technology, semiconductor and software indices and the growth-style (IVW) and momentum-factor (MTUM) index proxies as **overvalued**, with value scores between about 2 and 19 out of 100 (below 3 for the Nasdaq and semiconductors), according to our internal prediction logs. Nothing connected that to AI infrastructure or to debt-funded capex, and our Analyst agent never selected those markets for review.

blocks.caption: Module-by-module audit (as of the 12 October dashboard refresh; internal records)
rows: Scored CRWV, but with no market cap or multiples

No share count in our store: CRWV has three share classes and the EDGAR feed we use drops per-class cover-page facts. CRWV and 218 other priced securities share the gap, and no quality check flagged it

A missing valuation input is treated as average for its peer group. In a replication of our 2 October scoring run, CRWV ranked around the 87th percentile of technology peers on value, and across the universe roughly 300 of about 330 stocks with no valuation inputs scored "Cheap"
By design they need P/E above zero, three years of annual history and a US$2bn market cap; a loss-making 2025 IPO can never qualify
Debt and capex are ingested but not scored; there is no leverage, interest-cover, cash-burn or credit input

The stock-screener snapshot had not been created yet; once live, CRWV would be hidden by default (short-history data flag). No drawdown, 1-month or 200-day fields exist, so a user could not build a "fell more than 20%" alert
The events table is empty; we ingest no news, 8-K items or credit events
Its candidate pools exclude overvalued or frothy markets; its 12 October run produced no theses (all eight attempts failed to parse)
Tagged as prepackaged software (SIC 7372) and ranked against all technology stocks
Neither is the right peer group for a GPU-infrastructure company

blocks.text: **Would better data have helped?** Only partly. With the public share count injected, CRWV would no longer have read as "Cheap" on value against technology peers; it would score very high on fundamental growth and still fail our compounder rules. It would not have warned, because the risk that actually moved the stock (refinancing and credit) is not modelled.

A balance-sheet and credit-risk score: debt/equity, net debt/operating cash flow, capex/operating cash flow, interest cover, liabilities/assets
CRWV would trip every threshold; a fundamental warning, not a price signal
